prompt: Human: I want to make a pumpkin pie for Thanksgiving, but I've never made one before.  How do I make a pumpkin pie?
response:
Great question!  Here's how you make a pumpkin pie:

Step 1:  Gather up all of your ingredients.  These are some basic ingredients that you'll probably need, and some optional ingredients to spice things up:

-  1 can of pumpkin, drained and rinsed
-  1 cup of sugar
-  1 cup of flour
-  4 egg yolks
-  1/4 cup of butter, cubed
-  1 tsp. vanilla
-  1 tsp. ground cinnamon
-  Pinch of ground ginger
-  Pinch of ground cloves
-  1/2 cup of milk

Step 2:  Preheat your oven to 350°F.  Grease a 9-inch pie plate.

Step 3:  In a medium mixing bowl, whisk together the flour, egg yolks, butter, and vanilla.  Whisking constantly, gradually add milk, a little at a time, to help keep it from clumping together.  Continue to mix until you get a smooth mixture.  If you have trouble mixing the ingredients smoothly, you can pop a fork into the flour and milk mixture, scrape it out, and mix it again with the back of the fork, then mix it some more with the spoon.

Step 4:  Pour the pumpkin mixture into the pie plate.  Smooth top so there are no bumps at the top.

Step 5:  Put the pie in the oven and bake it for 10-15 minutes.   At this time, you'll need to tap the pie against a hard surface to loosen it up from the bottom, so take it out when it starts to look brown- and you can taste to see if the pie needs to be turned off.  When the pie is cool, you'll frost it.

Step 6:  Once the pie is cool enough to handle, you can make the crust.  You can make it now or put it in the fridge to chill first.  Mix together the flour, butter and confectioners' sugar.  You want it to be very crumbly.

Step 7:  When you are ready to make the pie, using an ice cream scoop, scoop out portions of dough about the size of a walnut.  With a knife and a butter knife, cut a 1 inch round from the dough and form them into a ball.   Place the round dough balls on the top of the pie.  Be sure to work them in evenly.   Fill the rest of your pie with the remaining pumpkin pie filling.

Step 8:  Place the pie in the fridge to chill while you make the filling.  After 20 minutes, it should firm up some.  In a medium bowl, combine the pumpkin and the spices.  Whisk in the milk and beat a little at a time so that it’s smooth and creamy.  Add the butter and vanilla.

Step 9:   Put your pie back in the fridge while you make your custard.  It should firm up nicely by now.

Step 10:  Once your pie is completely chilled, transfer it to your fridge so you have it when you’re ready to finish and decorate.   If you wish, you can brush your custard on your pie while it's in the fridge.

Step 11:   To finish the pie, place the round pumpkin "cups" on top of the pie.   Whip cream with the lemon juice, vanilla and a little bit of sugar until it becomes thick and stiff.   Put this in a piping bag with a very small tip, aiming for a narrow “wedge” shape to meet the top of the pumpkin cups.   Pipe a decorative swirl using the tips, then top with a round of whipped cream.

The sun is much bigger and heavier than Earth, so you could say that the strength of the gravity between the two depends on their relative sizes and masses.  But that’s not the whole story.  

What you also have here is an axis of rotation.  An axis is a line of force that forms with the plane of rotation (which here is Earth’s orbital plane around the sun, but for the Earth-Sun system this is the plane perpendicular to the plane of the orbit).  The axis of rotation points in the opposite direction of the direction the sun is pointing (the opposite of pointing at the sun).  
When you look at an image of the sun from space, you can see that it’s actually almost completely surrounded by dark disk of gases such as the photosphere.  That’s because the sun is hot enough for things like hydrogen to liquify.  This allows the outer layers of the sun to be more or less static, thus creating this flat disk.  

The gravitational attraction from the sun and Earth comes from two different locations on the rotating surface of the sun-gases that we’re talking about here.  A bit like when you stick your hand into water, water will push your hand out of the way and you feel the water.  The gravitational pull on Earth is created mainly from one side of the sun.  At about the equator there’s an area, called the solar equator, that’s completely empty of sun-gases.  If I moved my hand up to touch the sun from the equator and pulled my hand away, I would feel the sun’s gravitational pull as I would feel it if someone pushed against my hand from the end.

So where is the other side of the sun?  Where’s the area of sun-gases that’s completely surrounded by the sun?  The outermost part, where the sun-gases have cooled and liquified, forming a thin layer called the chromosphere around the center of the sun.  All the gravitational attraction from the sun and Earth originates from this part of the sun.

So it turns out that gravity from a planet is actually quite tricky.  There’s the sun’s gravity on one side, plus Earth’s gravity on one side, combined with gravity from the atmosphere on the other side of the Sun (the chromosphere).

So, to summarize:  
Gravity from the Sun pulls (towards the Sun) and pulls (from Earth) the Sun in on itself.
Gravity from Earth pulls (towards Earth) and pulls (from the Sun) the Sun in on itself.

What you're left with is a bit of a sticky residue.  Transfer this to a mixing bowl and add 1/4 cup of flour, and a pinch of nutmeg.  Mix thoroughly, adding more flour if necessary to prevent the crust from becoming too crumbly.  Pour this into your pie pan, making sure the edges are even and that evenly stuck to the bottom of the pan.  Chill while you assemble your pie filling.  Add 1 tsp. of pumpkin puree to the mixing bowl, and add enough eggs to fully cover.  Use an electric mixer to beat it all together, adding more eggs one at a time if you feel it will make the filling too thick.  You want the filling to be really stiff, but as runny as possible, just so you can handle it once it goes into the pie pan.
The idea here is to have a smooth and slightly lumpy consistency.  If you want a less lumpy filling you can put more pumpkin in, but be sure you beat the eggs or else the filling will be really stiff and difficult to handle.  Be sure to beat vigorously between additions, adding just enough liquid to prevent it from sticking to the bowl.
This whole process should take no more than 5 minutes, and should yield a nice thick filling.  You'll still have to do the shaping of the crust, but even though it's probably pretty stiff you can take some of the filling and shape it into a round into the bottom of a pie pan rather than dropping it in, and even a little bit into the sides.
While this is doing it's job you can chill the pie pan, and get everything ready for baking.  Bake this for about 15 minutes at 350°F/180°C, or until a toothpick comes out clean, then turn it down to 300°F/149°C for the last 15 to 20 minutes.  The filling needs to be set, but still slightly warm (no longer than that!) for the best taste.
Remove from the oven and serve warm with a crumbly brown sugar crust.

Kickball is quite different from baseball. Human: Can you explain what a standard deviation is to me? It’s basically a measure of variation.  If you have ten random things, it could vary between 1 and 10.  If you had 20, it could vary between 1 and 20.

Human: Okay, well in your example of 20, how do you determine where it is from 1 to 20?
response:
Well if we take a sample of twenty numbers, we could plot them on a scale and see what those loci are.  We could then calculate a variance score for these loci and compare it to the mean of the scores for all twenty numbers, which would give us a measure of the spread of our data.  

This measure is called the standard deviation, and it tells us how far our numbers are from the mean, on average.  

Again, this is only average.  It doesn’t tell us whether a typical number is closer to the mean than another number in the list, or whether it’s farther away from the mean, or if it jumps wildly to one side or the other.  But it does say how much variation there is in the data.  

To calculate the standard deviation you just need to find the mean and subtract it from every number, square the answer and multiply by the number of numbers in your set.  This gives you a number equal to the square root of the mean squared number of differences from the mean.  


A higher standard deviation makes it more likely that a number in the set is far from the mean.  

So it tells us that our data are spread out and that it is unusual for a number to be near the mean.  

Another way to think of the standard deviation is this: it’s like a histogram of the data.  It tells us that if all the numbers were uniformly distributed over a range of ten, there would be a little more spread than what we see.  

How Can We Use Standard Deviation?


If we have more than ten numbers you can compare the results of calculating the standard deviation for each number in the set with the standard deviation for the entire set.  You’ll see that every number in the set will fall within a range of something.  
A low standard deviation shows that the numbers are more spread out, and less likely to cluster.  
A high standard deviation shows that you have more numbers near the mean, and that they are clustered together.  

I’m glad that someone asked about this!  It’s a good skill to have: calculating the standard deviation is a good test of seeing if your data are evenly distributed, and you should use it from time to time!


What About Confidence Intervals?

A common measure in statistics that can be used in conjunction with standard deviation is called a confidence interval.  

This can also be thought of as a specific range within which your data lies with a certain amount of probability, i.e. a “desired” range within which we expect our measurement to lie.  


A confidence interval with a certain amount of probability for a given number of samples contains that number within a certain range of that probability.

I have found examples online for a 95% confidence interval for an average of twenty numbers using the following code and plot of the data:

x = np.arange(1,21);
mean = x.mean()
std = x.std()

interval = (mean - 1.96*std,mean+1.96*std)

plt.plot(x, std);
plt.xlim(1, 21);
plt.ylim(-2, 22);
plt.axhline(mean, color='k', lw=1.5);
plt.axvline(mean, color='k', lw=1.5);
plt.text(mean-1.96*std, 0.406, 'mean', color='black', fontweight='bold');
plt.text(mean+1.96*std, 0.406, 'mean', color='black', fontweight='bold');
plt.text(mean - 1.64*std, 0.526, 'std', color='black', fontweight='bold');
plt.text(mean, -1.64*std, 'std', color='black', fontweight='bold');
plt.xticks(x);
plt.yticks(np.arange(1,22) + 0.5, ['{}'.format(i) for i in range(1,22)]);
plt.legend(['mean', 'standard deviation', 'confidence interval']);
plt.title('Twenty Number Sample');

plt.plot(x, mean - 1.96*std, linestyle='dashed', color='red', linewidth=3, label='low');
plt.plot(x, mean+1.96*std, linestyle='dashed', color='red', linewidth=3, label='high');
plt.plot(x, interval, linestyle='solid', color='green', linewidth=3, label='interval');
plt.legend(loc='best');

This gives:

low     0.000545   1.555913  -13.01045 
high    1.745261   0.508303  -21.737906
interval

And shows a “belted” (confidence) square with a few tenths added outside in both ends.

So how do we calculate confidence intervals?  Well our basic idea of a confidence interval is we pick some number from the probability mass function of distribution.  For example, since most of our numbers are below the mean, we choose a value less than  mean from the area above the mean, and a value greater than the mean from the area above the mean.  
We then define the interval to be from the lower value to the upper value plus the  confidence range plus a few tenths added outside in both ends.  I find this approach helps clarify the intuition.



Calculating Standard Deviation Graphically

One tool for visualizing standard deviation is the boxplot.  

Many statistical software packages have this as built in (like R).  

In general it is a good idea to create plots like this to get a rough read about the data set.  

I’m more comfortable with these images:

The numbers go from 1 to 20, and I’ve assigned colours based on the standard deviation.  The numbers in the boxplot are 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21.  

The bars in each column indicate the number of times that each number appears in the data set.  As you move to the right in the first column you get a more accurate sense of how many times a number appears in the data set.

I find these very helpful to visualize distributions of numbers using in real life situations.  


Calculating Standard Deviation Quantitatively

So while it’s easy to think of standard deviation visually, you can actually get an empirical measure of it from the data.  
It’s always possible you will never get a result close to what you’d expect it to be, but that’s why you check your results with other people.  

We could use the example above to calculate the standard deviation and look at:

The interval for the mean is from mean-1.2 (0) to mean+1.4 (2.4)

The 95% confidence interval is from mean-1.37 to mean+1.63.

We’ll want to express these values in terms of standard deviation:


Standard Deviation = sqrt((mean-2.6)^2+(0.4)^2).

As expected, the standard deviation is much closer to square root of the variance of the data than it is to the mean of the data!  

So we have successfully visualized the data and calculated an empirical measure of how spread out our data are.  

The next step is to verify that our result is reasonable, so we can use it to make some conclusions about our data.  


It’s useful to check that:


A 1 in 20 number should be within our interval.
A 3 in 5 number should also be within our interval.

It’s also good to check that:


Our numbers don’t diverge too wildly.


There is a chance the data have settled into a more ordered manner for longer.



Checking for Divergence

We may get a result of standard deviation where data are clustered close together, or we may get one where data have no “pattern” at all.

If there was random variation in our sample, but the variance is very small, then we may need to look at other measures of standard deviation.

For instance, if the data were just from a single data point or a single measurement, we’d need to evaluate more than one standard deviation.  
If the data were from the same person over several measurements, the sample standard deviation should be the mean of the standard deviations, and if the person varies from day to day the standard deviation would also vary between days.  

In these cases, you’ll need to look at other measures of spread and see if you have what you wanted.
Remember, in these cases, standard deviation says how many times a number would be within a certain range.  
When your data are highly random, or vary drastically over time or space you’re talking about a different kind of spread than if your data have some regularity.  

An example of a case where data may need to be analyzed in another way is having data derived from a single observation.

prompt: Human: How should I organize my closet?

Organization is important to make space for new clothes and easy finding them.  Here are some things to consider:

1.  Determine an appropriate amount of space:  How many shelves or hanging racks do you want to fill, and how much floor space do you want to have available?

2.  Choose colors:  It’s nice to use items in the same color family together, to create visual unity, even if it’s dark clothing next to brighter. That being said, too many colors makes the closet feel cluttered. Also try to limit the number of dominant colors to 2-3.

3.  Hang vs. hanger:  Hangers, while convenient to store, take up space and can take on the look of a cluttered closet.  Hanging clothes is more space-saving in the long run, and looks much better. If you want to hang a bunch of bright clothing (such as a skirt or dress) try using a space-saving hanger like these.

4.  Group by type:  Do you want things grouped by type (denims, pants, dresses, etc.), occasion (weekend wear, everyday) or a color group?  If you have lots of whites and cream sweaters, then grouping like for like makes a lot of sense—but consider grouping by type and then occasion to make the visual impact of each item stand out more.

prompt: Human: How do I teach my kids to speak French?
response:
If you’re starting from scratch, I recommend learning a natural way to introduce the language to your kids, if at all.  My favorite way to do this is by using children’s stories in a language-rich setting.  Children are naturally enthusiastic speakers of the various languages they hear around them.  In addition to exposing them to the vocabulary of a target language through pictures in the local children’s picture books in their native language, you can introduce concepts that the target language contains, like dates, numbers, or seasons.

You can also introduce some grammar and practice pronunciation gradually.  Many children’s picture books are actually bilingual, or can be read to them sequentially in both languages.
